title: Ash Wednesday (Genesis 3:19)
hook: ashes on the forehead: dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ordinary Time, the long season of counted Sundays. Your line was green, growing. Which ordinary task did you do as if it mattered? Day one hundred forty-eight.

One Wednesday every year, usually in February or early March, you start seeing people around town with a dark smudge on their foreheads. The barista. A nurse on her lunch break. A guy on the subway. Someone at work might lean over and say, you've got something on your face. They know. It's on purpose. It's one of the busiest days of the year in Catholic churches, even though Catholics aren't required to attend Mass that day. Millions line up to be told something most of us spend our lives trying not to think about. Today: Ash Wednesday.
screen: `A SMUDGE ON THE FOREHEAD.` → `YOU'VE GOT SOMETHING ON YOUR FACE.` → `THEY KNOW.`

segments.voice: Ash Wednesday is the first day of Lent, about six and a half weeks before Easter. The ashes usually come from burning the palm branches from the previous year's Palm Sunday, so last spring's celebration becomes this spring's dust. The priest, deacon or minister dips a thumb in the ashes and traces a cross on each forehead, saying one of two sentences. One is from the Gospel of Mark: "repent, and believe the gospel." The other is older, and it's the one people remember. It comes from Genesis, when God speaks to Adam after the fall. In the Douay-Rheims: "for dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return." In the old Latin: Memento, homo, quia pulvis es, et in pulverem reverteris. Remember, man, that you are dust. That sounds grim at first. But listen to where it comes from. In Genesis, God forms the first human out of the dust of the ground and breathes life into him. Dust isn't an insult. It's what we're made of, and it's what God chose to breathe into. So the ashes say two things at once. You are going to die. And you are dust that God shaped by hand and filled with breath. That's today's line: dust, and loved. Catholics between eighteen and fifty-nine fast on Ash Wednesday, one full meal and two small ones, and everyone fourteen and older skips meat. The day isn't about being morbid. It's about being honest. Life is short, and knowing that plainly can make you kinder, braver, less hurried about things that don't matter. Other Christians keep it too: Anglicans, Lutherans, Methodists and more.
screen: `LAST YEAR'S PALMS, BURNED.` · `REPENT, AND BELIEVE THE GOSPEL.` · `DUST THAT GOD BREATHED INTO.` · `FASTING, AND NO MEAT.` · then, large: `DUST THOU ART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with your own mortality, kindly. Settle, and breathe. Touch your forehead lightly with your thumb, where the ashes would go. Let yourself think it: one day, I'll die. Don't rush past it, and don't spiral. Just notice. Then feel your breath going in and out, the same breath Genesis says God gave. If you pray, you can say, dust, and loved. If you don't, just let the plain fact make the next hour a little gentler. The bell holds the time.
Ash Wednesday. The first day of Lent, a cross of ashes on the forehead, and the words: dust thou art. Today's word.
Your line: dust, and loved. Today, because life is short, say one thing you've been saving to someone who should hear it. Day one hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: On Ash Wednesday Catholics go to church to receive a cross of ashes on the forehead, often wearing it through the day, and those old enough fast and abstain from meat.

original.note: Hebrew, Genesis 3:19: for dust you are, and to dust you shall return. Afar is dust, the stuff Adam was shaped from.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gloomy day for feeling bad.
what it means: an honest day: you will die, and you are dust that God shaped and breathed into. dust, and loved.
what a scholar hears: afar, dust, in Genesis 3:19 echoes Genesis 2:7, where God forms the human from the dust of the ground.

notes: Latin formula 'Memento, homo, quia pulvis es, et in pulverem reverteris' given in the voice without quotation marks. Confirm.
Fasting ages 18–59 and abstinence from 14 (canons 1251–1252); 'one full meal and two small ones' is the US norm. Confirm.
Ashes may be distributed by priests, deacons, and in some places lay ministers. Script says 'priest, deacon or minister'. Confirm.
